title: Vape Sales to Minors
stem: Sales of vapes to people under 18 should be banned in order to reduce teenage nicotine addiction.
answer_reason: Option A is the strongest because it links the proposed action (banning sales to under-18s) directly to the desired outcome (reducing teenage nicotine addiction) using empirical evidence from comparable jurisdictions. Option B addresses parental feelings rather than addiction rates. Option C makes an unsupported assumption about teenager behaviour and does not refute that the ban could reduce addiction overall. Option D addresses adult use, which is irrelevant to the teenage outcome in the proposition.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; in countries where vape sales to minors were restricted, follow-up surveys recorded a measurable fall in teenage nicotine addiction rates within five years of enforcement.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many parents would feel reassured if vapes were not legally sold to their children.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; teenagers will obtain vapes through informal channels regardless of formal restrictions.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some vapes are designed to help adults quit smoking and should remain commercially available.

title: Theatre Group Roles
stem:
A theatre group has 50 members. 12 members only act, 10 members only sing, and 5 members both act and sing. 15 members only dance — none of the dancers also act or sing. The remaining 8 members work backstage and do not act, sing, or dance.

Which of the following diagrams is consistent with the data?
answer_reason: The data describes one isolated category (dancing, with 15 members and no overlap with acting or singing) and two overlapping categories (acting with 12 only, singing with 10 only, and 5 in both). The correct diagram must show one shape completely separate from the other two, while the other two partially overlap. Option A matches: an isolated shape with 15 members, two overlapping shapes with 12-only, 10-only, and 5 in their overlap, plus 8 outside. Option B incorrectly places the dancing group as overlapping with another shape — the data states no such overlap. Option C swaps the overlap count (8) with the outside count (5), so 8 members would appear in both acting and singing instead of 5. Option D puts the largest only-region (15) on an overlapping shape and only 12 on the isolated shape — but the isolated shape must hold the dancing-only count of 15.

title: Greenhouse Ferns
stem: All ferns require shade unless they are mature. All mature ferns must be misted weekly. Some ferns in the greenhouse have not been misted weekly.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some ferns in the greenhouse are not mature.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Mature ferns must be misted weekly. Some greenhouse ferns have not been misted weekly, so by contrapositive those ferns cannot be mature.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All ferns in the greenhouse require shade.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The 'unless' rule means mature ferns do not require shade. Some greenhouse ferns might still be mature (those that have been misted weekly), so we cannot conclude every greenhouse fern requires shade.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All ferns that have been misted weekly are mature.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premise states mature ferns must be misted, not that every misted fern is mature. This is a reverse-inference error — non-mature ferns may also be misted.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some ferns in the greenhouse require shade.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: From statement 1 we established some greenhouse ferns are not mature. Non-mature ferns require shade, so some greenhouse ferns require shade.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No mature ferns are in the greenhouse.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We only know that some greenhouse ferns are not mature. The remaining greenhouse ferns could still be mature — the premises do not rule this out.

title: Marbles Without Replacement
stem:
A box contains 5 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement.

What is the probability that both marbles drawn are blue?
answer_reason: Total marbles = 5 + 4 + 3 = 12. P(first marble blue) = 4/12 = 1/3. After removing one blue marble, 3 blue marbles remain out of 11 total, so P(second blue | first blue) = 3/11. P(both blue) = 4/12 × 3/11 = 12/132 = 1/11. Distractor A (1/9) treats the draws as if with replacement (4/12 × 4/12). Distractor B (1/12) forgets to reduce the denominator from 12 to 11. Distractor D (2/11) doubles the conditional probability incorrectly.

title: Bookshop Stock
stem: A bookshop stocks 90 books across three sections: fiction, non-fiction, and poetry. There are 38 fiction books and 12 poetry books. Half of the non-fiction books are paperback. None of the fiction books are paperback. There are no paperback poetry books.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: There are 40 non-fiction books in the bookshop.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Total books = 90. Fiction = 38, poetry = 12. Non-fiction = 90 − 38 − 12 = 40.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: There are 25 paperback books in total.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Paperback only comes from non-fiction (fiction and poetry have none). Half of 40 non-fiction = 20 paperbacks. The total is 20, not 25.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: More than half of the books in the bookshop are not paperback.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Total paperbacks = 20 (all non-fiction). Non-paperbacks = 90 − 20 = 70. Half of 90 is 45, and 70 > 45.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All poetry books are hardback.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We are told there are no paperback poetry books, but the alternative format is not specified. Poetry could be hardback, e-book, or some other format — 'not paperback' does not equal 'hardback'.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All fiction books are hardback.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Same trap as the previous statement. Fiction is described as not paperback, but its actual format is not stated. We cannot conclude it is specifically hardback.

title: Office Committees
stem:
An office of 120 employees is split across four committees: Planning, Finance, Marketing, and IT. Each employee is on exactly one committee.

• Planning has half as many members as Finance.
• Marketing has 6 more members than IT.
• Finance has 40 members.

How many employees are on the IT committee?
answer_reason: Finance = 40 (given). Planning = 40 ÷ 2 = 20. So Marketing + IT = 120 − 40 − 20 = 60. Marketing = IT + 6, so (IT + 6) + IT = 60, giving 2 × IT = 54 and IT = 27. Marketing = 33. Check: 20 + 40 + 33 + 27 = 120. Distractors: A is the Planning value, B comes from forgetting the +6 and dividing 60 ÷ 2 incorrectly, D is the Marketing value.

title: Research Institute Staff
stem:
The diagram shows staff at a research institute categorised by Faculty membership, PhD status, active research grants, sabbatical leave, and external advisor status. Each letter marks a different region of the diagram.

Which letter represents a faculty member who holds a PhD and is currently the recipient of an active research grant?

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter Q

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter R

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter S

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter T

answer_reason: A faculty PhD holder with an active grant must lie inside the Faculty (rectangle), the PhD holders (square), and the Active grant recipients (circle) all at once. Region R is the triple overlap of those three shapes. Letter Q is faculty + PhD without a grant. Letter S is faculty + grant without a PhD. Letter T is faculty on sabbatical only. Only R satisfies all three conditions simultaneously.

title: Hospital Admissions
stem: If a patient has a fever above 39°C, they must be admitted for observation. Patients admitted for observation receive intravenous fluids. Some patients in the ward have not received intravenous fluids.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some patients in the ward do not have a fever above 39°C.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The chain is: fever above 39°C → admitted for observation → receives intravenous fluids. By contrapositive, anyone who has not received intravenous fluids cannot have a fever above 39°C. Some ward patients have not received fluids, so those patients do not have a fever above 39°C.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All patients receiving intravenous fluids have a fever above 39°C.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: This reverses the chain. The premises only say fever above 39°C leads to receiving fluids — they do not say receiving fluids requires a fever. Other reasons for receiving fluids may exist.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No patient in the ward has been admitted for observation.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We only know some ward patients have not received intravenous fluids. The remaining patients may well have been admitted for observation. We cannot conclude none have.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All ward patients with a fever above 39°C have received intravenous fluids.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Fever above 39°C → admitted → intravenous fluids. Any ward patient with such a fever must therefore have received intravenous fluids.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some patients in the ward have a fever above 39°C.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises do not establish that any current ward patient has a fever above 39°C. They only describe what happens if such a fever is present.

title: Compulsory Cycling Helmets
stem: Wearing a cycling helmet should be made compulsory for adult cyclists in the UK in order to reduce serious head injuries on the roads.
answer_reason: Option A directly addresses both the action (compulsory adult helmets) and the outcome (reduction in serious head injuries) with concrete evidence. Option B addresses cost and availability rather than head injuries. Option C addresses comfort, again not the head-injury outcome. Option D raises a tangential public health concern about exercise levels but does not contest the head-injury claim itself, making it weaker than A.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; data from countries that introduced adult helmet laws shows a measurable fall in cycling-related serious head injuries after enforcement began.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; helmets are inexpensive and widely available from retail shops.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some adults find helmets uncomfortable in warm weather.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; mandatory helmet laws may discourage cycling overall, reducing the broader public health benefits of regular exercise.

title: Rare Condition Screening
stem: A new diagnostic blood test for a rare condition has a sensitivity of 90% (correctly identifies 90% of people with the condition) and a specificity of 80% (correctly identifies 80% of people without the condition). The condition affects 1 in 200 people in the general population. Consider a randomly tested group of 4,000 people.
answer_reason: Out of 4,000 people, 4,000 ÷ 200 = 20 actually have the condition and 3,980 do not. True positives = 20 × 0.90 = 18, not 20, so A is wrong. False positives = 3,980 × 0.20 = 796, which rounds to about 800, so C is correct. The positive predictive value is 18 / (18 + 796) ≈ 2.2%, far below 50%, so B is wrong (a classic base-rate trap). Sensitivity is only 90%, so 10% of true cases are missed — D is wrong because a negative result cannot rule out the condition with certainty.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: About 20 people in the group will be true positives.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: A person who tests positive has a greater than 50% chance of actually having the condition.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: About 800 people in the group will receive a false positive result.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: A negative test result rules out the condition with certainty.

title: Office Break-In
stem:
Three colleagues — Peter, Quinn, and Ravi — are interviewed about an office break-in. Exactly one of them is the culprit. The culprit always lies; the other two always tell the truth.

• Peter says: 'Ravi is innocent.'
• Quinn says: 'I am innocent.'
• Ravi says: 'Quinn is lying.'

Who is the culprit?
answer_reason: Test each suspect. If Peter is the culprit, Peter lies, so 'Ravi is innocent' is false, making Ravi the culprit — contradiction. If Ravi is the culprit, Ravi lies, so 'Quinn is lying' is false, meaning Quinn tells the truth and is innocent; Peter (innocent) tells the truth, so Ravi is innocent — contradiction. If Quinn is the culprit, Quinn lies about being innocent (consistent), Peter truthfully says Ravi is innocent (consistent), and Ravi truthfully says Quinn is lying (consistent). Only Quinn produces a consistent assignment.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Peter

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Quinn

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Ravi

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Cannot be determined

title: Cafe Drink Add-Ons
stem:
A cafe sells 50 specialty drinks customised with three add-ons: caramel syrup, espresso shot, and oat milk. 12 drinks contain only caramel syrup, 10 only an espresso shot, and 8 only oat milk. 6 drinks combine caramel syrup and espresso shot. 4 drinks combine espresso shot and oat milk. No drink combines caramel syrup with oat milk. 10 drinks contain none of these add-ons.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Caramel-only = 12, espresso-only = 10, oat-milk-only = 8, caramel ∩ espresso = 6, espresso ∩ oat milk = 4, none = 10. Total = 50. The diagram must show espresso bridging caramel and oat milk (the only two pairwise overlaps), with no caramel ∩ oat milk region. Option A matches every value. Option B swaps the two overlap counts. Option C invents a caramel ∩ oat milk overlap (3 drinks) which the data forbids and reduces oat-milk-only to compensate. Option D swaps the caramel-only (12) and oat-milk-only (8) counts.

title: Paradox of Thrift
stem: Some economists argue for the 'paradox of thrift' — the theory that when many households in an economy save more, total demand falls and the economy contracts, eventually reducing aggregate savings. Critics counter that this only holds in the short run and ignores how savings finance investment in the long run. Most observers agree that during recent recessions, increases in household savings rates have coincided with falls in consumer spending.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Increased saving causes the economy to contract.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The paradox of thrift is described as a theory held by some economists, not as established fact. Critics dispute it. Treating it as a proven causal claim goes beyond what the passage supports.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Higher household saving rates and lower consumer spending have occurred together during recent recessions.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage explicitly states most observers agree this co-occurrence has been seen. It is presented as agreed-upon, not contested.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: In the long run, increased saving damages the economy.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Critics in the passage argue the opposite — that savings finance investment in the long run. The conclusion contradicts the only long-run claim the passage offers.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Total demand always falls when households save more.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: This treats the paradox of thrift as a universal law. The passage frames it as a contested theory and notes critics restrict it to short-run conditions only.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some economists believe that aggregate saving can ultimately reduce aggregate savings.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: This restates the paradox of thrift theory described in the passage as the view held by some economists.

title: Two Glucose Devices
stem:
Two laboratory devices measure blood glucose levels.

• Device X gives the correct reading 70% of the time. When the same blood sample is tested ten times in a row, Device X produces the same reading on 9 of those 10 trials.
• Device Y gives the correct reading 95% of the time. When the same blood sample is tested ten times in a row, Device Y produces the same reading on 5 of those 10 trials.

Which of the following statements is correct?
answer_reason: Accuracy is how often the device gives the correct reading: X = 70%, Y = 95%, so Y is more accurate. Precision is how consistently it gives the same reading on repeated trials: X = 9/10 = 90%, Y = 5/10 = 50%, so X is more precise. Therefore X is more precise but less accurate than Y, making C correct. A swaps the accuracy comparison. B swaps the precision comparison. D conflates two unrelated metrics — averaging accuracy does not affect precision.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Device X is more accurate than Device Y.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Device Y is more precise than Device X.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Device X is more precise but less accurate than Device Y.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: The two devices have equal precision when their accuracy is averaged.

title: Vornicks and Prozzlers
stem: All vornicks are quibbles unless they have been zilked. Most quibbles produce dranthe. No prozzler can produce dranthe. Some unzilked vornicks are prozzlers.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some vornicks do not produce dranthe.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Some unzilked vornicks are prozzlers, and no prozzler can produce dranthe. Therefore at least some vornicks (the prozzler ones) do not produce dranthe.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All quibbles are vornicks.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises only tell us unzilked vornicks are quibbles. They do not state the reverse — there may be quibbles that are not vornicks.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some prozzlers are quibbles.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Some unzilked vornicks are prozzlers, and unzilked vornicks are quibbles. Those individuals are therefore both prozzlers and quibbles.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All zilked vornicks produce dranthe.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises say nothing about what zilked vornicks do or whether they are quibbles. We cannot infer their dranthe production.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No quibble is a prozzler.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: From statement 3 we deduced some quibbles are prozzlers. This conclusion directly contradicts that, so it cannot follow.

title: Four-Day School Week
stem: Secondary schools in England should adopt a four-day school week in order to improve student wellbeing.
answer_reason: Option A is the strongest because it links the action (four-day week) to the outcome (student wellbeing) with direct, evidence-based outcome measures (stress and sleep quality). Option B addresses teacher workload, not student wellbeing directly. Option C is the closest competitor — it does engage with wellbeing — but its argument depends on a multi-step chain (less instruction → worse academic outcomes → anxiety) without supporting evidence for any link. Option D addresses parental childcare logistics, which is unrelated to the student wellbeing outcome.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; pilot schemes in three local authorities showed measurable improvements in student-reported stress levels and sleep quality after switching to a four-day week.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; teachers would also benefit from longer weekends, leading to better-prepared lessons across the school.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; reducing scheduled instruction may harm academic outcomes, and academic struggle is a recognised cause of teenage anxiety, undermining the wellbeing aim.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; many parents rely on schools for childcare on a Friday and would struggle to make alternative arrangements.

title: Hotel Occupancy
stem: A hotel chain recorded the percentage occupancy of its hotels in four UK cities across three quarters of 2025.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Manchester had the highest occupancy of the four cities in Q2.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Q2 occupancies: London 85, Manchester 72, Edinburgh 88, Bristol 68. Edinburgh's 88 is the highest, not Manchester's 72.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Bristol's occupancy increased by more than 10 percentage points between Q1 and Q3.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Bristol Q1 = 60, Q3 = 75. 75 − 60 = 15 percentage points, which is greater than 10.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Manchester's occupancy was higher than London's in every quarter.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: In Q1 London = 78 and Manchester = 65. London is higher, so Manchester was not higher in every quarter.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All four cities saw an increase in occupancy from Q1 to Q3.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: London 78 → 92, Manchester 65 → 80, Edinburgh 70 → 95, Bristol 60 → 75. All four ended Q3 above their Q1 figure.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Edinburgh's occupancy increase from Q1 to Q2 was greater than its increase from Q2 to Q3.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Edinburgh Q1 → Q2: 88 − 70 = 18 percentage points. Q2 → Q3: 95 − 88 = 7 percentage points. 18 > 7, so the first jump was larger.

title: Library Book Categories
stem:
The diagram shows books in a library categorised by genre. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a book that is classified as both Fiction and Poetry?

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter P

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter R

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter U

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Letter T

answer_reason: Fiction and Poetry form one overlapping pair, while Science and History form a separate overlapping pair, with no overlap between the two pairs. Region R sits in the overlap of the Fiction circle and the Poetry pentagon, representing books classified as both. Letter P is Fiction only. Letter T is History only (a different pair). Letter U is the Science ∩ History overlap, which is unrelated to Fiction and Poetry.

title: Friends and Sports
stem:
Four friends — Ada, Beth, Chris, and Dora — each play exactly one different sport from the following: tennis, golf, hockey, and swimming.

• Ada does not play hockey or swimming.
• Beth plays hockey.
• Chris does not play tennis.
• The friend who plays golf has a name ending in a vowel.

Who plays swimming?
answer_reason: Beth plays hockey (given). Ada does not play hockey or swimming, so Ada plays tennis or golf. Chris does not play tennis, so Chris plays golf or swimming. The golf player's name must end in a vowel: Ada and Dora qualify, Chris does not. So Chris cannot play golf — Chris must play swimming. (Either Ada plays tennis and Dora plays golf, or Ada plays golf and Dora plays tennis — either way, Chris plays swimming.)

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Ada

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Beth

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Chris

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Dora

title: Spinner Independent Events
stem:
A spinner is divided into 8 equal segments numbered 1 to 8. The spinner is spun twice, and each spin is independent.

What is the probability that the first spin lands on a multiple of 3 and the second spin lands on an even number?
answer_reason: Multiples of 3 between 1 and 8 are {3, 6}, so P(multiple of 3) = 2/8 = 1/4. Even numbers between 1 and 8 are {2, 4, 6, 8}, so P(even) = 4/8 = 1/2. The spins are independent, so P(both events) = 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8. Distractor A (1/16) miscounts multiples of 3 as one outcome. Distractor C (1/4) only uses the first event. Distractor D (3/8) wrongly adds the two probabilities.
